edge.relationship: First published in 1972 to develop feminist scholarship in conversation with the women’s movement, including historical research and early Berkshire Conference issues.
edge.evidence_note: An interdisciplinary women’s-studies institution with a documented women’s-history component. The edge does not restrict its programme to history or date the origin of women’s history to 1972; organizing began in 1969.

withdrawals.reason: Interdisciplinary feminist founding project; establish its constitutive relationship to women’s history specifically. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1975 to provide an interdisciplinary forum for the expanding scholarship on women, including historical inquiry and documentary recovery.
edge.evidence_note: Links the historical component of a broader feminist scholarly programme. This is neither a claim of exclusive disciplinary affiliation nor an origin date for all women’s history.

withdrawals.reason: Interdisciplinary women’s-studies institution; establish the women’s-history target rather than assume it. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1976 as an institutional forum for historical explanation drawing selectively on social-science theories and methods.
edge.evidence_note: An institutional project within the broad social-history expansion, with qualitative as well as quantitative methods. Its interdisciplinary scope exceeds this atlas entry; it does not endorse every approach listed in the entry.

withdrawals.reason: The cited constitution states a historical-social-science mission; field-forming role within new social history needs separate evidence. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1927 to develop economic and social historical inquiry, articulated in the first issue through Ashley’s programme and the journal’s original subtitle.
edge.evidence_note: Consolidates an existing field through a society journal. The programme included social history and cannot be reduced to later cliometrics; 1926 is the society’s foundation, not this first publication date.

withdrawals.reason: Plausible formative disciplinary institution; retain a distinction between establishment of the society/journal and much earlier economic history. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1973 as an annual forum combining Oral History Association colloquium papers and contributed articles for the developing practice of oral history.
edge.evidence_note: One institutional forum in a much older and internationally diverse practice. The US association, its newsletter and the separate British journal Oral History are not conflated.

withdrawals.reason: The launch announcement proves a publication mechanism, not by itself the journal’s constitutive role. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Founded in 1974 as a methodological forum for African history, emphasizing critical scrutiny of historical sources and the ways historians use them.
edge.evidence_note: A specific source-critical programme within African historiography, not the creation of African historical thought or an assignment of every African historian to one method. Claim limited to the available first-editorial extract.

withdrawals.reason: The methodological initiative is narrower than the existing African historiography target; do not call it the foundation of African history. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1989 to make gender’s historical experience and significance a focused programme of historical inquiry.
edge.evidence_note: Retrospective abstract-level evidence supports this limited founding-purpose claim. The target is the gender-history component of the combined Gender & racial formation entry; the edge does not date or subsume every racial-formation approach.

withdrawals.reason: Potentially constitutive for gender history; abstract evidence needs a fuller historical check, and target includes racial formation beyond this claim. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1970 to develop interdisciplinary historical methods, giving quantitative analysis a place within a wider exchange with the social sciences and other disciplines.
edge.evidence_note: The quantitative connection is one explicit component of a broader founding programme. The journal is not exclusively quantitative and the link does not equate its programme with all cliometric or serial-history approaches.

withdrawals.reason: The founding project was interdisciplinary history; quantification is a component, not necessarily the appropriate founding target. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1958 to create a forum for comparative inquiry across history and the social sciences, bringing specialists into discussion of recurring historical problems.
edge.evidence_note: Its comparative programme offers an institutional home for historical sociology but extends to anthropology and the humanities. The edge neither reduces the journal to sociology nor assigns it the later state-formation theories in this atlas entry.

withdrawals.reason: Founding comparative interdisciplinary forum is documented; the specific comparative-historical-sociology target needs justification. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1995 to consolidate interdisciplinary research and scholarly exchange on nations and nationalism through an association journal.
edge.evidence_note: A field-consolidating institution after earlier decades of nationalism scholarship, not the field’s beginning or an endorsement of a single explanation of nations.

withdrawals.reason: Evidence supplied is consolidation of an existing field; insufficient under the corrected founding criterion. Withdraw the founding claim; accept the separately evidenced sustained-venue relation.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1986 to provide an interdisciplinary forum for Holocaust research in conversation with the wider scholarly study of genocide.
edge.evidence_note: The edge connects the Holocaust component of a wider programme to the existing atlas entry. Comparative genocide studies is not thereby claimed to be comprehensively represented by that entry; the evidence is contemporary reception, not a full reading of the founding editorial.

withdrawals.reason: A later interdisciplinary venue; the evidence supplied does not establish a founding role for Holocaust studies. Withdraw the founding claim; retain the journal as a candidate for a sustained-venue review; the existing evidence is insufficient.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1984 to bring historians and anthropologists into a shared forum where each discipline could reconsider its methods through the other’s work.
edge.evidence_note: A particular institutional exchange, not the origin of historical anthropology. Distinct from Stocking’s History of Anthropology series, which the same contemporary review contrasts with this journal; intended collaboration does not prove that disciplinary divisions disappeared.

withdrawals.reason: Evidence supplied establishes disciplinary exchange, not the founding of anthropology or historical anthropology. Withdraw the founding claim; retain the journal as a candidate for a sustained-venue review; the existing evidence is insufficient.

edge.relationship: Launched in 1990 as the World History Association’s research journal to develop historical inquiry from a global perspective.
edge.evidence_note: The 1989 announcement directly states purpose and scheduled start; the accepted 1990 title record corroborates the launch. This is one institutional project within the atlas’s wider world/global/connected-history umbrella, not its unique origin or every later connected-history approach.

withdrawals.reason: WHA already existed and world history has earlier traditions. Replace the launch-based founding inference with a sourced institutional venue relation.

added_sources.note: Read pp. 1–2 on successive editors and the continuing comparative forum. The 2008 article summaries are not evidence of pre-2000 content; dated atlas articles supply earlier anchors.

added_sources.title: Immanuel Wallerstein, “The Rise and Future Demise of the World Capitalist System: Concepts for Comparative Analysis,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 16.4 (1974), 387–415.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source wallerstein_rise_primary. Original check: Read printed 387–400 and 411–415 using OCR; 401–410 unread. Named Braudel, Polanyi, Luxemburg, Frank/Santos and Sweezy resources; direct Rostow and Dobb criticism. The division-of-labor unit permits external arenas. Coerced-labor, agricultural-capitalism and future-system claims are arguments, not consensus. Final page endorses archival and quantitative work. Quoted originals and detailed semiperiphery mechanisms in unread pages not independently checked.

added_sources.title: Joan W. Scott and Louise A. Tilly, “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 17, no. 1 (1975): 36–64.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source scott_tilly_work. Original check: Publisher-hosted primary opening extract and original issue metadata read. Questions assumptions that domestic women were unproductive or that paid work and emancipation formed one linear sequence. Remainder of article and data unread; online 2009 date is not original publication.

added_sources.title: Sherry B. Ortner, “Theory in Anthropology since the Sixties,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 26.1 (1984), 126–166.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source ortner_practice_primary. Original check: Scan transcription of primary 126–128 and beginning 129 read; remaining essay unread. Page 127 calls practice an orientation embracing several theories/methods and explicitly locates the author’s perspective. Publisher metadata at Cambridge confirms January 1984, not 2009 online date. Platform-generated summary ignored; cited genealogies are Ortner’s assessments.

added_sources.title: Hans Medick, “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? Ethnological Ways of Knowing as a Challenge to Social History, Comparative Studies in Society and History 29(1) (1987): 76–98.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source medick_missionaries. Original check: Cambridge primary opening and notes checked at https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/comparative-studies-in-society-and-history/article/abs/missionaries-in-the-row-boat-ethnological-ways-of-knowing-as-a-challenge-to-social-history/3FC3FA5BAC8CA59E26CB341A4A24075D . Introductory note engages Bernard Cohn’s critique of ahistorical anthropology; note 10 documents the working group since 1978 and Medick/Sabean, Interest and Emotion (1984). This substantiates a particular exchange; full article and earlier German version unread.

added_sources.title: Anne E. C. McCants, Editor’s Introduction to Volume 40, Issue 1 (2016)
added_sources.note: Read retrospective account of forty years of SSHA’s journal, continuity of analytical commitments and expanding international scope. Includes both qualitative and quantitative methods.

added_sources.note: Read longitudinal discussion of issues from 1913, 1924, 1934, 1944, 1954, 1984 and 1994, and the late-century assessment. The existing 1912 foundation / 1913 first-volume distinction is preserved.

added_sources.note: Accepted-manuscript founding and development sections read, including early contributions, the 1996 Miller symposium, ongoing lectures and institutional editorial continuity. Later statistics are not used to rank its 1990s importance.

added_sources.note: Interview read on the journal’s 1960 origin, editorial continuity from 1965, and recurring theory/philosophy theme issues. Self-description as the leading journal is not adopted as a measured ranking.

added_sources.note: Publisher abstract read, not the full article. It explicitly describes sustained importance, changing methods and Stearns’s continuing defence of social history. Selection is limited to that longitudinal abstract claim.

added_sources.title: Raphael Samuel, “Local History and Oral History,” History Workshop Journal 1(1) (1976): 191–208.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source samuel_local_oral. Original check: OUP bibliographic record checked. added_sources.title: Doreen Massey, Places and Their Pasts, History Workshop Journal 39(1) (1995):182–192.

Publisher confirms date, pages and Spatial History section. Supports contested place histories, explicit Gilroy use and criticism of Harvey 303, independently checked here. added_sources.title: Past & Present, Celebrating Issue 250: selected articles and editorial commentaries (2021)

added_sources.title: Michel R. Doortmont, Making History in Africa: David Henige and the Quest for Method in African History (2011), 7–20
added_sources.note: Read pp. 7–9 and 14–20: review of 36 volumes, source criticism and archival reports. Retains 1974 volume dating while noting the author’s April 1975 appearance date; no canonical chronology is changed.

added_sources.title: SHOT, Melvin Kranzberg: participant memorials
added_sources.note: Read recollections of journal editing, manuscripts, institutional development and the 1981 editorial handover; retrospective participant evidence, not a complete article census.

added_sources.title: World History Bulletin 28.2 (2012), Jerry Bentley remembrance
added_sources.note: Search-indexed retrospective passage read: the journal’s central role from its 1990 launch through Bentley’s editorship. Direct PDF now returns 404 and archive endpoint unavailable. No claim to have read the complete tribute.

added_sources.title: American Society for Environmental History, History: Publications
added_sources.note: Read institutional account of successive society journals and editors. This supports institutional continuity; title boundaries use the separately accepted publisher/JSTOR review.

added_sources.title: David Bloor, “Anti-Latour,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 30.1 (1999), 81–112.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source bloor_anti_latour_primary. Original check: Downloaded original journal PDF. Read introduction 81–82, section-three opening 87–88, agency discussion 91–92, central symmetry paragraph on 102 and conclusion 110–111; additional adjoining passages read without claiming complete intervening pages or full article. Bloor distinguishes beliefs about nature from nature, includes material causes, and rejects equal credibility as the meaning of symmetry. His assessments of Latour and historical examples remain attributed claims. Final rejoinder at 131–136 unread. Additional reading in1.65: complete90 and opening91, including the response to Latour’s Pasteur example. Bloor proposes asking about interpretive resources and contrasts Koch’s response; historical case claims remain his.

added_sources.title: Bruno Latour, “For David Bloor… and Beyond,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 30.1 (1999), 113–129.
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source latour_bloor_reply_primary. Original check: Original journal PDF from author archive: complete 113–120 and opening 121 read, not remainder. DOI 10.1016/S0039-3681(98)00039-9 matches PubMed; 00038-7 belongs to Bloor. Page 114 and note 2 provide explicit debt and mediation testimony. Earlier CiteSeer, Melissa and legacy-page fetches failed; original located through author catalogue page 15. Claims about opponents and French epistemology remain Latour’s interpretations, not independent verdicts; translation credits are not separately collated.

added_sources.title: Anthony D. Smith and Ernest Gellner, Warwick debate, 24 October 1995; published in Nations and Nationalism (1996).
added_sources.note: Reused atlas source warwick_nationalism. Original check: Primary Smith opening read on the LSE resource page; Gellner’s reply at https://www.lse.ac.uk/researchAndExpertise/units/gellner/Warwick2.html consulted for cultural continuity and modern mobility/literate culture. The linked introduction dates the event to 1995, distinct from publication. Smith credits Gellner’s teaching but disputes sufficiency of modernist explanation; neither position is a consensus. Gellner’s provocative primordialist label does not define Smith’s own qualified ethno-symbolic position.

added_sources.title: Ernest Gellner, reply to Anthony D. Smith in the Warwick debate (published 1996)
added_sources.note: LSE primary reply consulted, previously read for atlas source warwick_nationalism. Event took place in October 1995; journal publication in 1996 is the venue date.
